# Marcus

Marcus sits in the waiting room fifteen minutes early for his appointment, scrolling through his phone with the kind of mechanical precision that suggests he's not really seeing what's on the screen. At fifty-six, he carries himself with the careful posture of someone who has learned to take up less space. His suit is well-maintained, his tie perfectly knotted—the uniform of professionalism he's worn for nearly a decade managing social media campaigns for a mid-sized marketing firm.

Three years ago, Marcus was driving home from work on a Thursday evening. He'd been thinking about his daughter's college tuition, about a client presentation scheduled for the following morning, about stopping at the market for his wife's favorite olives. He was pulled over for a broken taillight on a street he'd driven a hundred times before. He remembers the officer approaching his window, remembers keeping his hands visible on the steering wheel—his father had taught him this years ago, a precaution for a brown man in America. He remembers asking politely what the problem was.

What happened next unfolds in his mind now as a series of fragmented moments rather than a coherent sequence. There was shouting. His door was yanked open. He was pulled from the car, and when he didn't move fast enough—when his body, confused and compliant, didn't respond to commands he could barely hear over the blood rushing in his ears—he was thrown against the hood. His face struck the metal. There was pain, then numbness. Later, there would be apologies, a settlement, acknowledgment of "excessive force." But in that moment, there was only the weight of a body pinning him down and the absolute certainty that something terrible was happening to him.

The charges were dropped. The incident report was filed. Marcus returned to his life.

Except he didn't, not really.

Now, when he drives, his hands grip the wheel so tightly his knuckles blanch white. He takes only main roads, well-lit streets, routes he's mapped obsessively in his mind. He's late to meetings because he's chosen longer drives over shorter ones. His boss has noticed his work slipping—the creative spark that once made him valuable has dimmed. He stares at his screen for hours, supposed to be crafting engaging content, but instead he's reading news stories about police encounters, watching videos, falling down rabbit holes of other people's trauma.

At night, he lies awake beside his wife, who has learned not to touch him without warning. When he does sleep, he wakes gasping, his shirt soaked through. The dreams are vivid and terrible—variations on that Thursday, each one ending differently, each one ending worse. Some nights he doesn't sleep at all. He sits in his study with the lights on, checking his phone, scrolling through social media feeds he's supposed to be managing but can't quite focus on.

His wife says he's changed. She means it gently, but he hears the worry underneath. His daughter calls less often—he's become someone who flinches at unexpected sounds, who needs to know where exits are in every room. He's aware of how his anxiety has become a presence in their home, a fourth person at the dinner table.

He tells his therapist that he knows, logically, that he's safe. He knows the incident is over. But his body hasn't received that memo. His nervous system remains convinced that danger is always moments away, that authority figures are threats, that the world is fundamentally unsafe. And he carries this knowledge, this hypervigilance, into every moment of his day—when he's managing social media campaigns, when he's driving, when he's trying to sleep, when he's trying to be the husband and father his family deserves.
